name: LMT86 analog temperature sensor
description: Precision CMOS analog temperature sensor from Texas Instruments. Its output falls about 10.9 mV per °C (2616 mV at −50 °C, 2100 mV at 0 °C, 1831 mV at 25 °C, 420 mV at 150 °C, slightly parabolic, per the datasheet transfer table), is specified from −50 °C to +150 °C, runs on 2.2–5.5 V and draws only 5.4 µA. Sold as: Texas Instruments LMT86LP bare TO-92 sensor, 3 straight legs with the flat face towards you: VDD, OUT, GND.
eli5: A tiny three-legged thermometer whose middle leg puts out a voltage that drops by about 11 millivolts for every degree warmer (2.1 V at freezing, 1.83 V at room temperature), so your board can read the temperature with its analog input. It runs happily on 3.3 V.

pins.name: VDD
pins.description: Supply, 2.2 V to 5.5 V (pin 1, left with the flat face towards you). 3.3 V is fine.

pins.name: OUT
pins.description: Analog temperature output (pin 2, middle): falls as temperature rises, 2.616 V at −50 °C, 1.831 V at 25 °C, 0.42 V at 150 °C (datasheet Table 7-1). Safe for a 3.3 V ADC.

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Ground (pin 3, right); also the die's thermal connection.

buildNotes: Pin order with the flat face towards you, legs down: left = VDD, middle = OUT, right = GND (datasheet Figure 5-3, TO-92 LP/LPM). The TO-92S version LMT86LPG is different (OUT, GND, VDD): check the part number.
Power VDD from 3.3 V: the LMT86 works from 2.2 V to 5.5 V. The output never exceeds 2.62 V, so it can go straight to a 3.3 V ADC pin.
The output FALLS as it gets warmer: 2.100 V = 0 °C, 1.831 V = 25 °C, 1.668 V = 40 °C. Convert with the datasheet transfer table (the driver does this).
Put a 0.1 µF capacitor between VDD and GND close to the sensor. A filter capacitor on OUT must be 1.1 nF or less unless you add a series resistor (3 kΩ up to 99 nF).
Average many ADC samples: one degree is only about 11 mV. On the ESP32 use an ADC1 pin with 11 dB attenuation.
The GND leg is tied to the die, so the sensor reads the temperature of its leads and board. Keep it away from the regulator and the MCU.

driver.code:
# LMT86 analog temperature sensor (Texas Instruments), MicroPython driver.
# Datasheet SNIS169F (May 2024): VDD = 2.2-5.5 V, 5.4 uA, push-pull output, power-on time 1.9 ms max.
# The output FALLS as temperature rises: 2616 mV at -50 C, 2100 mV at 0 C, 1831 mV at 25 C,
# 420 mV at 150 C (average gain -10.9 mV/C). The response is slightly parabolic, so the driver
# interpolates the datasheet's Transfer Table (Table 7-1), which TI gives for host look-up tables
# and which is the reference the accuracy specs are stated against.
from machine import ADC, Pin

# Table 7-1: VOUT in mV for every whole degree from -50 C to +150 C.
_T0 = -50
_MV = (
    2616, 2607, 2598, 2589, 2580, 2571, 2562, 2553, 2543, 2533,  # -50..-41 C
    2522, 2512, 2501, 2491, 2481, 2470, 2460, 2449, 2439, 2429,  # -40..-31 C
    2418, 2408, 2397, 2387, 2376, 2366, 2355, 2345, 2334, 2324,  # -30..-21 C
    2313, 2302, 2292, 2281, 2271, 2260, 2250, 2239, 2228, 2218,  # -20..-11 C
    2207, 2197, 2186, 2175, 2164, 2154, 2143, 2132, 2122, 2111,  # -10..-1 C
    2100, 2089, 2079, 2068, 2057, 2047, 2036, 2025, 2014, 2004,  # 0..9 C
    1993, 1982, 1971, 1961, 1950, 1939, 1928, 1918, 1907, 1896,  # 10..19 C
    1885, 1874, 1864, 1853, 1842, 1831, 1820, 1810, 1799, 1788,  # 20..29 C
    1777, 1766, 1756, 1745, 1734, 1723, 1712, 1701, 1690, 1679,  # 30..39 C
    1668, 1657, 1646, 1635, 1624, 1613, 1602, 1591, 1580, 1569,  # 40..49 C
    1558, 1547, 1536, 1525, 1514, 1503, 1492, 1481, 1470, 1459,  # 50..59 C
    1448, 1436, 1425, 1414, 1403, 1391, 1380, 1369, 1358, 1346,  # 60..69 C
    1335, 1324, 1313, 1301, 1290, 1279, 1268, 1257, 1245, 1234,  # 70..79 C
    1223, 1212, 1201, 1189, 1178, 1167, 1155, 1144, 1133, 1122,  # 80..89 C
    1110, 1099, 1088, 1076, 1065, 1054, 1042, 1031, 1020, 1008,  # 90..99 C
    997, 986, 974, 963, 951, 940, 929, 917, 906, 895,  # 100..109 C
    883, 872, 860, 849, 837, 826, 814, 803, 791, 780,  # 110..119 C
    769, 757, 745, 734, 722, 711, 699, 688, 676, 665,  # 120..129 C
    653, 642, 630, 618, 607, 595, 584, 572, 560, 549,  # 130..139 C
    537, 525, 514, 502, 490, 479, 467, 455, 443, 432,  # 140..149 C
    420,  # 150..150 C
)


def mv_to_celsius(mv):
    """Convert an LMT86 output voltage (mV) to C by linear interpolation of Table 7-1."""
    if mv >= _MV[0]:
        return float(_T0)          # at or below -50 C (end of the specified range)
    if mv <= _MV[-1]:
        return float(_T0 + len(_MV) - 1)  # at or above 150 C
    lo, hi = 0, len(_MV) - 1       # binary search on the falling table
    while hi - lo > 1:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if _MV[mid] > mv:
            lo = mid
        else:
            hi = mid
    v1, v2 = _MV[lo], _MV[hi]
    return _T0 + lo + (v1 - mv) / (v1 - v2)


class LMT86:
    def __init__(self, pin, samples=32, vref=3.3):
        self.adc = ADC(Pin(pin) if isinstance(pin, int) else pin)
        try:
            self.adc.atten(ADC.ATTN_11DB)  # ESP32: 0-3.1 V range covers the 0.42-2.62 V output
        except AttributeError:
            pass
        self.samples = samples
        self.vref = vref  # ADC reference used when read_uv() is not available (e.g. Pico)

    def millivolts(self):
        """Average several ADC samples and return the output voltage in mV."""
        total = 0
        if hasattr(self.adc, 'read_uv'):
            for _ in range(self.samples):
                total += self.adc.read_uv() / 1000
        else:
            for _ in range(self.samples):
                total += self.adc.read_u16() * self.vref * 1000 / 65535
        return total / self.samples

    def temperature(self):
        """Temperature in C from the datasheet transfer table."""
        return mv_to_celsius(self.millivolts())

# LMT86 analog temperature sensor (LMT86LP)

## Overview
The **LMT86** (Texas Instruments) is a precision CMOS temperature sensor with an analog voltage output. It has no digital interface: you read the output with an ADC. Hobbyists buy the **LMT86LP** in a 3-pin TO-92 package (straight leads; LMT86LPM has formed leads, same pinout).
- Output **falls** as temperature rises: average gain **−10.9 mV/°C**
- Output: **2616 mV at −50 °C**, **2100 mV at 0 °C**, **1831 mV at 25 °C**, 997 mV at 100 °C, **420 mV at 150 °C**
- Specified **−50 °C to +150 °C**
- Accuracy: ±0.4 °C typical (40–150 °C), ±0.7 °C typical (0–40 °C, VDD ≥ 2.4 V), ±2.7 °C max
- Supply: **2.2 V to 5.5 V**, only **5.4 µA**, push-pull output (±50 µA), power-on time 0.7 ms typ / 1.9 ms max

## Pinout (TO-92 LP/LPM, flat face towards you, legs down)
| Pin | Name | Function |
|-----|------|----------|
| 1 (left) | VDD | Supply, 2.2–5.5 V |
| 2 (middle) | OUT | Analog output (falls with temperature) |
| 3 (right) | GND | Ground (also the die's thermal path) |

From datasheet Figure 5-3 and Table 5-1. **The TO-92S version (LMT86LPG) has a different order: 1 OUT, 2 GND, 3 VDD.** Check the part number before wiring.

## Electrical limits
- Supply: 2.2 V min, 5.5 V max (absolute max −0.3 V to 6 V).
- Output: −0.3 V to VDD + 0.5 V absolute; ±50 µA drive. The output never exceeds 2.62 V, so it is safe for a 3.3 V ADC.
- Keep VDD − VOUT ≥ 200 mV: at −50 °C the output is 2.62 V, so a 3.3 V supply is fine (2.2 V only works down to about −5 °C).
- Capacitive load up to 1100 pF directly; larger capacitors need a series resistor (3 kΩ for 1.1–99 nF, 1.5 kΩ for 100–999 nF, 800 Ω for 1 µF).

## Interface details
The response is very linear but slightly parabolic. The reference is the datasheet **Transfer Table (Table 7-1)**, one mV value for every degree from −50 to 150 °C; the driver interpolates it.
The datasheet's parabolic approximation (Equation 1, off by up to 10 mV at the extremes):
```
VOUT(mV) = 1777.3 − 10.888 × (T − 30) − 0.00347 × (T − 30)²
```
Examples from Table 7-1: 2.100 V = 0 °C, 1.831 V = 25 °C, 1.668 V = 40 °C, 1.558 V = 50 °C, 0.997 V = 100 °C.
For a quick linear estimate over 20–50 °C the datasheet gives V(mV) = −10.9 × T + 2103.

## Wiring
| Sensor | ESP32 | Raspberry Pi Pico | Raspberry Pi 4 |
|---|---|---|---|
| VDD | 3V3 | 3V3(OUT) (pin 36) | 3.3 V (pin 1) |
| OUT | GPIO34 (ADC1) | GP26 / ADC0 (pin 31) | External ADC input (e.g. MCP3008 CH0 or ADS1115 A0) |
| GND | GND | GND | GND |

The Raspberry Pi 4 has **no built-in ADC**, so you need an external ADC. On the ESP32 use ADC1 pins (ADC2 does not work while Wi-Fi is on). Add a 0.1 µF bypass capacitor across VDD/GND and, for a sampling ADC, a small filter capacitor (≤ 1.1 nF without series resistor) on OUT (datasheet Figure 8-1).

## Using the driver
```python
from lmt86 import LMT86
import time
sensor = LMT86(26)          # GPIO number of the ADC pin OUT is wired to
while True:
    print('T=%.1fC' % sensor.temperature())
    time.sleep(1)
```
The driver averages 32 samples. It uses calibrated `read_uv()` where the port has it (ESP32), otherwise `read_u16()` × 3.3 V / 65535 (pass `vref=` if your 3V3 rail is different). `mv_to_celsius(mv)` converts a voltage you measured some other way (e.g. with an ADS1115).

## Gotchas
- **The output goes DOWN when it gets warmer.** Formulas for LM35/TMP36 give nonsense here.
- **Pin order differs between packages:** TO-92 (LP/LPM) is VDD-OUT-GND, TO-92S (LPG) is OUT-GND-VDD.
- **Low power:** at 5.4 µA you can power it from a GPIO and switch it off between readings; wait 2 ms after power-on before reading.
- **Resolution:** about 11 mV/°C. A 12-bit 3.3 V ADC gives about 0.07 °C per step. Average samples.
- **Pico ADC reference** is the 3.3 V rail: if it sags, readings shift. Pass the measured rail as `vref=`.
- **Placement:** the GND leg is tied to the die, so board heat flows straight into the reading. Keep it away from the regulator and MCU.
